sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: The system records advertisement clicks and redirects users to advertisers. Advertisers query the recorded click totals.
Redirects must remain fast. Separate click collection from aggregation so analytics work does not delay redirects.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Users can click an ad and reach its configured destination.
Advertisers can query click totals over time. The smallest requested interval is one minute.
Count one click for each ad impression. Ad targeting, ad serving, and advanced fraud detection are outside the scope.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: The example has 10 million active ads and a peak of 10,000 clicks per second. Analytics queries should take less than one second.
Retain accepted click events durably. The system must recover counts after a processor failure.
Advertisers need recent totals. Precompute aggregates so each query does not scan all raw events.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: An Ad record identifies the advertiser and redirect URL. The Ad Placement Service supplies this metadata.
A ClickEvent contains an event ID, ad ID, user ID when available, and timestamp.
A MinuteAggregate contains an ad ID, minute timestamp, and click count. Retain raw events for reconciliation.

sections.title: API and Data Flow
points: The /click endpoint records a click and returns a 302 redirect. The browser then requests the advertiser's URL.
A metrics endpoint accepts an ad ID and time range. It returns counts for the requested time intervals.
The Click Processor uses the destination associated with the ad. The browser does not choose an arbitrary redirect destination.
The data path is click collection, durable storage, aggregation, then analytics queries. Later designs add a separate raw archive.

sections.title: 1) Click ingestion
points: The browser sends the ad click to the Click Processor. The processor records the click before returning the redirect.
A direct browser redirect with a separate tracking request is simpler. However, users can reach the destination without recording a click.
Server redirects add a request to the path. Define what happens when recording fails; a fast redirect alone does not prove durability.

flows.title: Record a click before redirecting
steps: The browser sends the ad click to the Click Processor.
The Click Processor obtains the redirect URL associated with the ad.
The processor records the click through the selected storage path. The next section compares those paths.
The processor returns a 302 response with the destination URL.
The browser follows the redirect to the advertiser.

sections.title: 2) Aggregation
points: The basic design writes raw clicks to an analytics database. Queries count matching records, which becomes expensive as traffic grows.
A batch design writes events to Cassandra. Scheduled Spark jobs aggregate them into an OLAP database, but results lag between jobs.
A streaming design sends events through Kafka or Kinesis to Flink. Flink groups events by ad and event-time minute.
Flink writes aggregates to the OLAP database. Watermarks and a late-event policy handle delayed events; frequent flushes expose provisional counts.

diagrams.caption: Store and Query From the Same Database

flows.title: Count raw events at query time
steps: The Click Processor writes each event to the Analytics DB.
An advertiser requests counts for an ad and a time range.
The Analytics Service queries the matching raw events and groups them by time interval.
The service returns the counts. This scan becomes expensive as event history and query traffic grow.

flows.title: Build counts with scheduled batches
steps: The Click Processor writes raw events to Cassandra.
The cron Scheduler starts a Spark job at the configured interval.
Spark reads the events and groups them by ad ID and minute.
Spark writes the aggregates to the OLAP DB.
The Analytics Service reads those aggregates for advertiser queries. Results remain stale until the next batch finishes.

flows.title: Maintain counts with stream processing
steps: The Click Processor writes events to Kinesis or Kafka.
Flink reads the events and assigns them to ad ID and event-time windows.
Flink updates each window's count and handles delayed events under the configured policy.
Flink writes aggregates to the OLAP DB. Frequent flushes can expose provisional totals before a minute finishes.
The Analytics Service reads the stored totals for the advertiser.

sections.title: 1) Scale ingestion and hot ads
points: A load balancer distributes clicks across Click Processor instances. Partition the stream and Flink work by ad ID.
A popular ad can overload one partition. Add a suffix to its partition key, then combine counts under the original ad ID.
Batch aggregate updates to reduce database writes. Choose a flush interval that meets the required freshness.
Monitor stream lag and available capacity. The OLAP database must combine partial counts without losing or repeating updates.

sections.title: 2) Durability and reconciliation
points: Replicate the stream and retain events for recovery. The example uses seven days of retention; small windows can be replayed.
Flink checkpoints preserve processing state. Recovery also needs a sink that handles replay without counting an event twice.
Archive raw events in S3. Scheduled Spark jobs recompute totals, and a Reconciliation Worker compares them with streaming results.
Correct affected OLAP records from the reconciled totals. Do not add the same historical count again during replay.

flows.title: Reconcile streaming totals with raw events
steps: An independent stream consumer archives raw click events in S3.
A scheduled Spark job reads an archive interval and recomputes its totals.
The Reconciliation Worker compares those totals with the OLAP DB results.
The worker investigates differences and updates affected records with corrected totals.
Repeated reconciliation must replace or safely update those records. It must not add the same historical totals again.

sections.title: 3) Abuse and repeated clicks
points: A user/ad pair is too broad for deduplication. The same user can legitimately see a new instance of the same ad.
The Ad Placement Service generates a unique impression ID. It signs the impression ID and ad ID before sending the ad.
The Click Processor verifies the signature and checks a Redis cache. It writes new clicks to the stream before caching their IDs. Reconciliation handles duplicates that survive a failure.

flows.title: Count one click for each impression
steps: The Ad Placement Service creates an impression ID and signs it together with the ad ID.
The browser sends that identity and signature with the click.
The Click Processor verifies the signature and checks the Redis cache for a previously accepted impression.
For a new impression, the processor writes the click to the stream before adding its ID to the cache.
Reconciliation handles duplicates that survive a race or cache failure. Advanced fraud detection remains outside this design.

sections.title: 4) Query latency
points: Query precomputed OLAP records by advertiser, ad, and time. This avoids repeated raw-event scans.
Precompute daily or weekly totals for long queries. Keep minute totals available when advertisers need finer detail.
Recent windows can be incomplete. Expose their freshness so advertisers know that the latest counts can change.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The Click Processor verifies impression IDs, records clicks, and redirects users. Kinesis or Kafka retains the accepted events.
Flink maintains minute aggregates in the OLAP database. S3, Spark, and the Reconciliation Worker provide a separate correction path.
The Analytics Service reads precomputed totals. Partitioning, impression deduplication, and reconciliation support scale and accurate counts.
